passage:
Leela's phone buzzed with a forwarded poster from Chetan: "guaranteed profit every week", with a screenshot of someone's payout. Underneath he had typed, "My cousin's already in, this is real. Join before Friday!"

Leela felt her stomach tighten. Chetan was the friend who had lent her his notes all semester, and he meant well. She didn't send a joke back. She searched the scheme's name, found no sign of who ran it and a long page of complaints, then called him instead of texting.

"I looked it up, Chetan, and I can't find who's behind it. Could you ask your cousin where the money actually goes?"

He was quiet. "I just don't want to miss out."

"I know. I'm not joining, but come for chai tomorrow?"

"...Fine. Bring the notes back."

qa.q: Who had forwarded the poster to Leela?
qa.a: Chetan forwarded the poster, which promised "guaranteed profit every week".

qa.q: What does Chetan mean when he says "I just don't want to miss out"?
qa.a: Chetan is afraid of losing a chance that his cousin seems to be enjoying, so he believes in the scheme because he does not want to be left behind.

qa.q: What could Leela try next if Chetan keeps forwarding the scheme?
qa.a: Leela could keep asking calm questions about who runs it and where the money goes, share what she found, and keep meeting him while still refusing to join.

qa.q: How might Leela see Chetan's forwarded poster?
qa.a: Leela sees Chetan as a friend who means well, but the poster worries her, since she found no sign of who ran the scheme and a long page of complaints.

grounding: A friend forwards a guaranteed-profit scheme he believes in, and Leela checks the source, questions calmly and keeps the friendship while refusing.

'Jomon, just listen for two minutes. It's a guaranteed eight percent a month. My cousin's friend is already earning.'
'Eight percent a month, Raghav? Guaranteed?'
'That's why it's so good. And if you bring two people, you get a bonus.'
'Who runs it?'
'Some trading company abroad. There's a video.'
'Is it registered with anyone here? Can we look it up?'
Raghav hesitated. 'I didn't check. But my cousin's friend showed me his screen.'
'Screens can show anything.' Jomon kept his voice easy. 'Look, I'm not saying you're dumb. I'm saying anything that promises that much, with no risk, and pays you for bringing people in, is exactly how the scams we read about worked.'
'So you're out.'
'I'm out of the scheme. I'm not out of chai with you.' He pushed a cup across. 'Before you put in more, let's look it up on the regulator's site together. Tonight.'
Raghav stared at the cup. 'Fine. Tonight.'

qa.q: What return did Raghav say was guaranteed?
qa.a: Raghav said it was a guaranteed eight percent a month.

qa.q: How does Jomon feel about Raghav while refusing the scheme?
qa.a: Jomon feels concerned but fond of Raghav, careful not to make him feel dumb.
He questioned calmly, suggested checking the regulator's site together, and kept the friendship while refusing the scheme.

qa.q: How might Raghav see Jomon's questions at first?
qa.a: Raghav may feel doubted and defensive, since he believes in the scheme and trusts his cousin's friend.

grounding: Shows a friend who sincerely believes in a guaranteed-profit scheme, and Jomon questioning calmly, suggesting a source check and keeping the friendship while saying no.

passage: I'm Farhan, and last spring my oldest friend Ashok sent me a voice note at midnight, breathless: a 'crypto mining' app that doubled your money in thirty days, guaranteed. He had already put in his scholarship money and wanted me in. I almost joined because it was him. Ashok isn't a cheat; he's the kid who returned a lost wallet in Class 6. He believed it. My sister Rashmi, who works at a bank, looked at the app with me the next morning. No registered company, no address, and the 'withdraw' button only worked after you invited three people. I called Ashok. I didn't say 'scam' first; I asked, 'Have you managed to withdraw anything?' He hadn't. I told him what we'd found, and that I wasn't joining. He was angry for a week. Then the app vanished. He called me, and we sat on his terrace for a long time. I'm glad I said no without saying goodbye.

qa.a: The app claimed it doubled your money in thirty days, guaranteed.

qa.q: What did Farhan feel toward Ashok when the voice note came?
qa.a: Farhan felt trust and loyalty toward Ashok, and was tempted to join just because it was him.

qa.q: How did Farhan question Ashok without attacking him?
qa.a: By calmly asking whether Ashok had managed to withdraw anything, then sharing what was found and refusing to join.

qa.q: What was it like for Ashok when Farhan refused?
qa.a: Ashok was angry for a week, probably hurt and defensive because he believed in the scheme.

grounding: A first-person account of a trusted friend caught up in a 'guaranteed' scheme, and checking the source, questioning calmly and keeping the friendship while refusing.
